title: Compare R&D tax advisors
description: When comparing R&D tax credit advisors, weigh competence and independence, fee basis, audit support terms, documentation practices and credentials.
summary: When comparing R&D tax credit advisors in the USA, businesses should weigh competence and independence, because the taxpayer stays legally liable for any IRC § 41 credit on its return. Advisor quality affects penalty protection under Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4, so check fee basis, audit support terms, documentation practices, credentials and readiness for Form 6765 Section G reporting.

body.text: When comparing R&D tax credit advisors in the USA, businesses should weigh competence and independence, because the taxpayer stays legally liable for any IRC § 41 credit on its return. Advisor quality affects penalty protection under Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4, so check fee basis, audit support terms, documentation practices, credentials and readiness for Form 6765 Section G reporting.
1. Why the choice of R&D tax advisor carries risk for the taxpayer
1.1 The taxpayer stays liable for the return

In IR-2024-31, issued February 1, 2024, the IRS states that taxpayers are ultimately legally responsible for all the information on their income tax return, no matter who prepares it. The IRS Taxpayer Advocate Service gives the same warning in its guidance on choosing a return preparer: the taxpayer is responsible for everything on the return even when someone else prepares it. Any research credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 that an advisor calculates ends up on the company's own return, on Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities, so the advisor's methods directly affect the company's exposure to adjustments, interest and penalties.

This point matters more for research credit work than for routine return preparation. An R&D credit study is usually prepared by a specialist firm and then carried onto a return that a different preparer signs, or onto an amended return filed as a claim for refund. In either case the company signs under penalties of perjury, and the specialist's work becomes the company's position. When the IRS examines the credit, the company must defend the qualified research expenses, the business components and the four-part test analysis that the advisor assembled.
1.2 Relying on an advisor does not automatically protect against penalties

The rule sits in Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4, which governs the reasonable cause and good faith exception to the accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662. Under § 1.6664-4(b)(1), reliance on the advice of a professional tax advisor does not by itself show reasonable cause and good faith. It does so only if, under all the circumstances, the reliance was reasonable and the taxpayer acted in good faith. Section 1.6664-4(c)(1) says all facts and circumstances must be considered, and gives an example: reliance may fail if the taxpayer knew, or reasonably should have known, that the advisor lacked knowledge in the relevant aspects of Federal tax law.

The courts have built a working test on top of the regulation. In Neonatology Associates, P.A. v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 43 (2000), the Tax Court held that a taxpayer relying on professional advice must show three things: the advisor was a competent professional with sufficient expertise to justify reliance; the taxpayer gave the advisor necessary and accurate information; and the taxpayer actually relied in good faith on the advisor's judgment. Courts have also added a requirement of independence. In 106 Ltd. v. Commissioner, 136 T.C. 67, 79 (2011), aff'd, 684 F.3d 84 (D.C. Cir. 2012), the Tax Court said advice must generally come from a competent and independent advisor who is not burdened with a conflict of interest, quoting Mortensen v. Commissioner, 440 F.3d 375, 387 (6th Cir. 2006). In 106 Ltd., the court found the advisors were promoters of the transaction, and held that relying on them was unreasonable. The regulation text reviewed does not itself mention conflicts of interest; that standard comes from case law.

A second penalty is relevant to advisors who prepare research credit refund claims. IRC § 6676 imposes a penalty of 20 percent of the excessive amount when a claim for refund or credit is made for an amount that exceeds the amount allowable, unless any part of the excessive amount is due to reasonable cause. Many R&D credit engagements produce amended returns for open years, so the competence of the advisor preparing the claim bears on this penalty as well as on the § 6662 penalty for original returns.

Analysis: When companies compare R&D tax advisors, the advisor's competence and independence decide whether the company can rely on that advisor's advice if a penalty is proposed. An advisor whose fee depends on the size of the credit, or who also sells the product being recommended, may be treated as conflicted, and that weakens the reliance defense.
2. What buyers say they look for when comparing advisors
Both concern consumer financial advisors, not R&D tax consultants. They can show general buyer priorities only, and they say nothing directly about how companies choose research credit specialists.

cells: YouGov Financial Services CategoryView (interviews with more than 9,000 US adults aged 18 and over, March to June 2024)

27% of Americans currently work with a financial advisor or planner. 60% named trustworthiness as the most important factor in choosing a financial advisor. Among higher-income adults (above 200% of median income) the figure was 68%, against 55% for lower-income adults.

2022 Granum Center for Financial Security Consumer Survey (The American College of Financial Services; national online survey of 1,157 consumers with at least $25,000 invested; results announced May 25, 2022)

Characteristic most often ranked first: evidence of knowledge (education, certifications) at 27.2%. "Trustworthy" was ranked first by 20.1%, and "ability to listen to and understand your goals" by 18.9%. Only about 8% ranked positive recommendations from people they know first.

body.text: Analysis: The Granum result is the more useful of the two for a company comparing R&D advisors, because it separates knowledge from trust. For research credit work, evidence of knowledge means demonstrable competence in IRC § 41, the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4 rules on qualified research, and the IRS's current filing and refund-claim requirements described in Sections 4 and 7. That is also the competence that Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(c)(1) makes relevant to penalty protection.
3. The cost of poor advice: what the evidence actually measures
3.1 The "$17 billion" figure

The figure comes from the CEA's February 2015 report The Effects of Conflicted Investment Advice on Retirement Savings, released on February 23, 2015. It estimates what conflicted investment advice costs IRA savers. The CEA found that savers receiving conflicted advice earn returns roughly 1 percentage point lower each year, and applied that to an estimated $1.7 trillion of IRA assets invested in products that generally pay conflicted fees, giving about $17 billion a year. It is not an estimate for poor advice in general, and it says nothing about tax advice. The CEA itself said a far more conservative assumption, half a percentage point, would still indicate annual losses of more than $8 billion, and that the total would exceed $17 billion if more IRA assets were affected or other retirement savings were included. NERA Economic Consulting disputed the estimate in a March 2015 review, and the Department of Labor published a response to that review.
3.2 CFP Board 2025 survey

A CFP Board news release dated June 10, 2025 reports a 13-question survey sent on April 7 and 8, 2025 to randomly selected Americans aged 25 to 64, sourced through Alchemer. It generated 1,044 responses, with a sampling error of plus or minus 3.0 percentage points at the 95% confidence level. The release reports that 39% of Americans lost $250 or more because of bad advice and 18% lost more than $1,000. The figures for delayed major decisions (33%), acting without professional input (29%) and unnecessary fees (28%) are shares of the 57% of respondents who reported regrettable decisions based on misleading online information. They are not shares of all Americans. The release is about consumer financial misinformation online, not business tax advice.
3.3 The Roth conversion malpractice example

The Journal of Accountancy (March 2025) describes a case in which a CPA casually mentioned Roth conversions during a tax-return review and did not document the conversation. The client converted traditional IRAs to a Roth IRA, faced a six-figure tax bill, and sued the CPA for the extra tax, penalties and loan interest. The claim investigation found no written record of the discussions, which weakened the CPA's defense. The article gives neither the exact amount nor the outcome. The case is a CPA professional-liability example, not an R&D credit case.

Analysis: None of these statistics measures losses from R&D tax advice specifically. They support only a general point: conflicted or undocumented advice has real costs. That is a reason to compare advisors on independence and documentation practices. They do not put a dollar figure on R&D-specific risk, and a report comparing R&D tax advisors should not present them as if they did.
4. Comparing fee structures

What the IRS release says. In IR-2024-31, the IRS advises taxpayers to avoid return preparers who base their fees on a percentage of the refund. That advice appears as a tip in the release, not in its list of red flags. The release's red flags section names two warning signs: a paid preparer who will not sign the return, which the IRS says is a red flag that the preparer is likely not to be trusted and may be chasing quick profits through big refund promises or fees tied to refund size; and "ghost preparers," who prepare a return but will not sign it as the paid preparer. The release also reminds taxpayers that anyone paid to prepare or help prepare federal returns must have a valid Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN) and must sign and include it on the return, and that preparer misconduct can be reported on Form 14157, Complaint: Tax Return Preparer.

Cash-only payment appears in AARP's consumer list of preparer red flags, which is a secondary source. On receipts, the IRS release makes a different point: it says good preparers ask to see records and receipts. A preparer who does not ask for supporting documents is the warning sign, which for R&D work translates into an advisor who does not ask for payroll, project and technical records.

The federal rules on contingent fees. Circular 230, the Treasury regulations governing practice before the IRS (31 C.F.R. Part 10), restricts contingent fees in § 10.27. A practitioner may not charge an unconscionable fee in connection with any matter before the IRS, and § 10.27(b) generally bars contingent fees, with limited exceptions such as services rendered in connection with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, a return, and judicial proceedings. Contingent fees for preparing original returns have been barred since 1994; the 2007 amendments extended the bar to amended returns and refund claims. In Ridgely v. Lew, No. 1:12-cv-00565 (D.D.C. July 16, 2014), the court held that the IRS lacked statutory authority to regulate contingent fees for preparing and filing ordinary refund claims, meaning claims filed after the original return but before an audit begins, and permanently enjoined enforcement of § 10.27 as to those claims. The court relied on Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014). The IRS did not appeal. CPAs and attorneys remain subject to their own professional and state ethics rules, which may still restrict contingent fees for tax return and refund-claim work.

Analysis: The IRS consumer guidance is written for return preparers. Applying it to R&D credit consultants who prepare credit studies is an analogy. The concern is the same: a fee that grows with the credit gives the advisor a reason to maximize the credit rather than its defensibility, and, under the case law in Section 1.2, a fee tied to the outcome can be relevant to whether the advisor was independent. Because Ridgely removed the federal bar for ordinary refund claims, contingent-fee R&D engagements on amended returns are lawful under Circular 230, so the buyer has to weigh the incentive rather than rely on a regulatory prohibition. When comparing R&D advisors, ask whether the fee is fixed, hourly or contingent; whether the advisor is a CPA, attorney or enrolled agent subject to professional ethics rules on contingent fees; and whether audit support costs extra.
5. Comparing external credentials: what they do and do not prove

cells: NASBA National Registry of CPE Sponsors

Registry sponsors provide continuing professional education (CPE) under the Statement on Standards for Continuing Professional Education Programs jointly issued by NASBA and the AICPA. All 55 State Boards of Accountancy accept CPE credit from Registry sponsors. NASBA approves a sponsor by delivery method after reviewing a submitted course; it does not review every course a sponsor offers.
NASBA states that Registry approval does not involve review of all of a sponsor's courses. The status is evidence of compliance with CPE standards, not an endorsement of a firm's R&D tax methodology.

Accreditation means the Better Business Bureau has found that the business meets its accreditation standards, including a commitment to make a good-faith effort to resolve consumer complaints. Accredited businesses pay a fee. BBB policy states that it does not endorse any product, service or business.

An A+ rating is evidence about business conduct and complaint handling. It does not measure technical tax quality, and a BBB profile reflects the specific legal entity and location listed, which may not match a group's full history.

The IRS says paid preparers must have a valid PTIN, and that enrolled agent status can be checked through IRS.gov or the IRS Directory of Federal Tax Return Preparers with Credentials and Select Qualifications. CPAs, attorneys and enrolled agents have unlimited representation rights before the IRS under Circular 230.
Included because representation rights determine whether the advisor who prepared the credit study can itself represent the company in an IRS examination of the claim.

body.text: 7. A checklist for comparing R&D tax advisors (analysis)

items: Competence in the relevant tax law. If the advisor lacks it, relying on their advice may not establish reasonable cause (Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(c)(1); Neonatology Associates, 115 T.C. 43).

Command of current Form 6765 reporting. The IRS released final Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) in February 2026. Section G, Business Component Information, was optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and is required for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, with exceptions including qualified small businesses electing the payroll tax credit and certain filers with total qualified research expenses of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less. An advisor preparing 2026 credits should be able to explain how it will collect component-level data.

Refund-claim requirements. Since January 10, 2022, a research credit claim for refund must include specified items of information to be valid. Interim guidance issued in January 2025 (LB&I-04-0125-0001) reduced the required items from five to three by removing the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the information each individual sought to discover, though the IRS may request those in an examination. The transition period that gives taxpayers 45 days to perfect a deficient claim runs through January 10, 2027 (IR-2025-99). An advisor preparing amended-return claims should know these rules and the § 6676 penalty for excessive refund claims.

Independence and conflicts of interest. Case law expects a competent, independent advisor without a conflict (106 Ltd., 136 T.C. 67, aff'd, 684 F.3d 84). Ask whether the advisor promotes or profits from anything beyond the fee.

Fee basis. Fixed, hourly or contingent? The IRS warns against fees tied to the size of the refund. Contingent fees for ordinary refund claims are no longer barred by Circular 230 after Ridgely v. Lew, but professional ethics rules may still apply, and an outcome-based fee bears on independence.

Audit support terms. Is defense included, conditional or billed separately? Read the written terms rather than the marketing. Check whether the advisor, or someone it engages, holds the credentials needed to represent the company before the IRS.

Documentation practice. Does the advisor put its advice in writing, and does it ask for payroll, project and technical records? (See the Journal of Accountancy example and the IRS point that good preparers ask to see records and receipts.)

Credentials, read precisely. NASBA sponsor status and a BBB rating are worth checking on the issuer's own site. They speak to CPE compliance and business conduct, not technical quality. Check which legal entity a BBB profile covers.

Self-reported claims. Size, longevity, "most conservative" status and audit record should be confirmed independently where possible, and the jurisdiction checked (for example, Australian versus IRS audits).

body.text: 8. Conclusion (analysis)

The taxpayer carries the liability for the return, and the advisor's competence and independence affect whether reliance on that advisor protects against the accuracy-related penalty and the penalty for excessive refund claims. Those two factors are therefore sound grounds for comparing R&D tax advisors. The $17 billion figure concerns conflicted IRA investment advice. There is no IRS advisor-"disqualification" mechanism; the governing standard is reasonable reliance under Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4 and the case law built on it. The IRS's percentage-of-refund warning is a tip rather than one of its listed red flags, and the federal contingent-fee bar no longer applies to ordinary refund claims after Ridgely v. Lew. NASBA and BBB status do not certify tax methodology. A buyer comparing advisors should test each firm's claims against primary sources in the same way, and should confirm that any advisor it hires is ready for the Section G reporting that applies from the 2026 tax year.
